references.title: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) as pleiotropic physiological signalling agents
references.finding: H2O2 and superoxide, made by >40 enzymes incl. NOX and the mitochondrial ETC, act at nanomolar levels as physiological signals ('oxidative eustress'); higher levels cause damage ('distress').

references.authors: Sies H
references.title: Hydrogen peroxide as a central redox signaling molecule in physiological oxidative stress: Oxidative eustress
references.finding: Defines physiological H2O2 (~1-10 nM) as oxidative eustress; higher levels trigger adaptive responses via Nrf2/KEAP1 and NF-kB; >100 nM causes biomolecular damage (distress).

references.authors: Sies H
references.title: Oxidative stress: a concept in redox biology and medicine
references.finding: Frames oxidative stress as a redox-signalling concept and states that antioxidant enzymes, not small-molecule antioxidants, fulfil the major role in defence.

references.authors: Murphy MP
references.title: How mitochondria produce reactive oxygen species
references.finding: Mitochondrial superoxide comes mainly from complex I and is high only with high protonmotive force/reduced CoQ or high NADH/NAD+; rates from isolated mitochondria cannot be extrapolated to in vivo.

references.authors: Holmström KM, Finkel T
references.title: Cellular mechanisms and physiological consequences of redox-dependent signalling
references.finding: ROS signal through reversible oxidation of specific cysteine residues and regulate many physiological cell-fate decisions.

references.authors: Winterbourn CC
references.title: Reconciling the chemistry and biology of reactive oxygen species
references.finding: Kinetic analysis of which oxidants react with which targets in cells; highlights that reactivity and compartmentalisation determine antioxidant effectiveness.

references.authors: Rhee SG, Woo HA, Kil IS, et al.
references.title: Peroxiredoxin functions as a peroxidase and a regulator and sensor of local peroxides
references.finding: Peroxiredoxins act as locally constrained peroxidases and can be inactivated to let H2O2 accumulate for signalling, and transfer oxidation to target proteins as H2O2 sensors.

references.authors: Bedard K, Krause KH
references.title: The NOX family of ROS-generating NADPH oxidases: physiology and pathophysiology
references.finding: Describes the NOX family (NOX1-5, DUOX1/2), the only enzymes whose primary function is ROS generation, and their physiology and pathology.

references.authors: Pacher P, Nivorozhkin A, Szabó C
references.title: Therapeutic effects of xanthine oxidase inhibitors: renaissance half a century after the discovery of allopurinol
references.finding: Xanthine oxidase generates superoxide and H2O2 and its inhibition (allopurinol, febuxostat) has therapeutic effects in conditions involving oxidative stress.

references.authors: Pacher P, Beckman JS, Liaudet L
references.title: Nitric oxide and peroxynitrite in health and disease
references.finding: Nitric oxide reacts with superoxide to form peroxynitrite, a potent oxidant/nitrating agent implicated in cardiovascular, inflammatory and neurodegenerative disease.

references.authors: Winterbourn CC
references.title: Toxicity of iron and hydrogen peroxide: the Fenton reaction
references.finding: The iron/H2O2 Fenton reaction generates hydroxyl radicals and higher iron oxidation states capable of oxidising a wide range of biomolecules.

references.authors: Dixon SJ, Stockwell BR
references.title: The role of iron and reactive oxygen species in cell death
references.finding: Iron-catalysed ROS initiate and mediate several forms of cell death, including ferroptosis.

references.authors: Dixon SJ, Lemberg KM, Lamprecht MR, et al.
references.title: Ferroptosis: an iron-dependent form of nonapoptotic cell death
references.finding: Identified ferroptosis, an iron-dependent, lipid-peroxidation-driven form of nonapoptotic cell death, inhibited by ferrostatin-1.

references.authors: Ayala A, Muñoz MF, Argüelles S
references.title: Lipid peroxidation: production, metabolism, and signaling mechanisms of malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal
references.finding: Reviews lipid peroxidation chemistry and the formation, metabolism and signalling roles of MDA and 4-HNE.

references.authors: Cooke MS, Evans MD, Dizdaroglu M, et al.
references.title: Oxidative DNA damage: mechanisms, mutation, and disease
references.finding: Oxidative DNA lesions such as 8-oxoguanine are mutagenic and repaired by multiple pathways; biomarker shortcomings explain inconsistent disease associations.

references.authors: Lu SC
references.title: Glutathione synthesis
references.finding: Glutathione is the most abundant non-protein thiol; synthesis is limited by cysteine availability and glutamate-cysteine ligase activity.

references.authors: Halliwell B
references.title: Understanding mechanisms of antioxidant action in health and disease
references.finding: Reviews endogenous, dietary and synthetic antioxidants, why most antioxidant trials failed, and the special antioxidant role of the gastrointestinal tract.

references.authors: Forman HJ, Zhang H
references.title: Targeting oxidative stress in disease: promise and limitations of antioxidant therapy
references.finding: Antioxidants work in preclinical models but clinical trials are disappointing; rational targeting requires understanding where and when oxidants cause pathology.

references.authors: Harman D
references.title: Aging: a theory based on free radical and radiation chemistry
references.finding: Original proposal of the free-radical theory of aging.

references.authors: Pérez VI, Bokov A, Van Remmen H, et al.
references.title: Is the oxidative stress theory of aging dead?
references.finding: Of 18 genetic manipulations of antioxidant enzymes in mice, only Sod1 deletion altered lifespan, challenging the oxidative stress theory of aging.

references.authors: Kensler TW, Wakabayashi N, Biswal S
references.title: Cell survival responses to environmental stresses via the Keap1-Nrf2-ARE pathway
references.finding: Nrf2-knockout mice are markedly more sensitive to toxicants, inflammation, cigarette smoke and carcinogens; KEAP1 retains and represses Nrf2 under quiescent conditions.

references.authors: Yamamoto M, Kensler TW, Motohashi H
references.title: The KEAP1-NRF2 System: a Thiol-Based Sensor-Effector Apparatus for Maintaining Redox Homeostasis
references.finding: Comprehensive review of KEAP1 as a cysteine-based redox sensor and NRF2 as the effector transcription factor; inducibility relies on rapid de-repression.

references.authors: Cuadrado A, Rojo AI, Wells G, et al.
references.title: Therapeutic targeting of the NRF2 and KEAP1 partnership in chronic diseases
references.finding: NRF2 activation protects against many chronic diseases; one NRF2 activator is clinically approved and others are in development; context matters in cancer.

references.authors: Kobayashi A, Kang MI, Okawa H, et al.
references.title: Oxidative stress sensor Keap1 functions as an adaptor for Cul3-based E3 ligase to regulate proteasomal degradation of Nrf2
references.finding: KEAP1 is an adaptor for a Cul3 E3 ligase that keeps Nrf2 half-life under 20 minutes by proteasomal degradation.

references.authors: Dinkova-Kostova AT, Talalay P
references.title: Direct and indirect antioxidant properties of inducers of cytoprotective proteins
references.finding: Distinguishes direct antioxidants (consumed, can be pro-oxidant) from indirect antioxidants that induce long-lived catalytic cytoprotective proteins via Keap1/Nrf2/ARE.

references.authors: Forman HJ, Davies KJ, Ursini F
references.title: How do nutritional antioxidants really work: nucleophilic tone and para-hormesis versus free radical scavenging in vivo
references.finding: Kinetic constraints make in vivo radical scavenging by nutritional antioxidants ineffective; their benefit is better explained by Nrf2 activation ('para-hormesis') maintaining nucleophilic tone.

references.authors: Wakabayashi N, Itoh K, Wakabayashi J, et al.
references.title: Keap1-null mutation leads to postnatal lethality due to constitutive Nrf2 activation
references.finding: Keap1-null mice with constitutive Nrf2 activation die postnatally from oesophageal/forestomach hyperkeratosis; rescued by Nrf2 deletion.

references.authors: Shibata T, Ohta T, Tong KI, et al.
references.title: Cancer related mutations in NRF2 impair its recognition by Keap1-Cul3 E3 ligase and promote malignancy
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Somatic NRF2 mutations disrupting KEAP1 recognition occur in human cancers, especially in smokers and squamous cell carcinoma, and confer poor prognosis and drug resistance.

references.authors: DeNicola GM, Karreth FA, Humpton TJ, et al.
references.title: Oncogene-induced Nrf2 transcription promotes ROS detoxification and tumorigenesis
references.finding: Oncogenic KRAS, BRAF and MYC raise Nrf2 transcription to lower ROS and promote tumorigenesis in mice.

references.authors: Wang XJ, Sun Z, Villeneuve NF, et al.
references.title: Nrf2 enhances resistance of cancer cells to chemotherapeutic drugs, the dark side of Nrf2
references.finding: Nrf2 overexpression made cancer cells resistant to cisplatin, doxorubicin and etoposide; Nrf2 knockdown sensitised them.

references.authors: de Zeeuw D, Akizawa T, Audhya P, et al.
references.title: Bardoxolone methyl in type 2 diabetes and stage 4 chronic kidney disease
references.n: 2,185 patients with type 2 diabetes and stage 4 CKD
references.finding: The potent Nrf2 activator bardoxolone methyl did not reduce ESRD or CV death and increased heart-failure hospitalisation or death (HR 1.83); trial terminated early.

references.authors: Gold R, Kappos L, Arnold DL, et al.
references.title: Placebo-controlled phase 3 study of oral BG-12 for relapsing multiple sclerosis
references.finding: Dimethyl fumarate (BG-12) reduced the annualised relapse rate by ~50% versus placebo over 2 years.

references.authors: Marzec JM, Christie JD, Reddy SP, et al.
references.title: Functional polymorphisms in the transcription factor NRF2 in humans increase the risk of acute lung injury
references.finding: A functional NRF2 promoter SNP (-617 C/A) lowered promoter activity and was associated with higher risk of acute lung injury after trauma (OR 6.44).

references.authors: Calabrese EJ, Kozumbo WJ
references.title: The hormetic dose-response mechanism: Nrf2 activation
references.finding: Proposes Nrf2 activation as a general mechanism of hormetic dose responses, with a quantitatively constrained, modest maximal stimulation; exercise and caloric restriction are activators.

references.authors: Bao Y, Wang W, Zhou Z, et al.
references.title: Benefits and risks of the hormetic effects of dietary isothiocyanates on cancer prevention
references.finding: Sulforaphane at 1-5 uM increased proliferation and migration of several human cell lines (to 120-143%), while 10-40 uM inhibited them: a biphasic, hormetic effect.

references.authors: Saw CL, Cintrón M, Wu TY, et al.
references.title: Pharmacodynamics of dietary phytochemical indoles I3C and DIM: Induction of Nrf2-mediated phase II drug metabolizing and antioxidant genes and synergism with isothiocyanates
references.finding: In HepG2 cells, low concentrations of indoles (I3C, DIM) combined with isothiocyanates (SFN, PEITC) induced ARE-mediated genes synergistically or additively.

references.authors: Zhang Y, Talalay P, Cho CG, et al.
references.title: A major inducer of anticarcinogenic protective enzymes from broccoli: isolation and elucidation of structure
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Isolated sulforaphane as the major inducer of anticarcinogenic phase 2 enzymes in broccoli.

references.authors: Fahey JW, Zhang Y, Talalay P
references.title: Broccoli sprouts: an exceptionally rich source of inducers of enzymes that protect against chemical carcinogens
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: 3-day broccoli sprouts contain 10-100 times more glucoraphanin than mature plants, and sprout extracts reduced mammary tumours in rats.

references.authors: Egner PA, Chen JG, Wang JB, et al.
references.title: Bioavailability of Sulforaphane from two broccoli sprout beverages: results of a short-term, cross-over clinical trial in Qidong, China
references.finding: Sulforaphane bioavailability was ~70% from a sulforaphane-rich beverage versus ~5% from a glucoraphanin-rich one; glucoraphanin gave slower elimination and more interindividual variability.

references.authors: Egner PA, Chen JG, Zarth AT, et al.
references.title: Rapid and sustainable detoxication of airborne pollutants by broccoli sprout beverage: results of a randomized clinical trial in China
references.finding: Daily broccoli sprout beverage (600 umol glucoraphanin + 40 umol sulforaphane) for 12 weeks increased benzene (+61%) and acrolein (+23%) detoxification; bioavailability did not decline over time.

references.authors: Chen JG, Johnson J, Egner P, et al.
references.title: Dose-dependent detoxication of the airborne pollutant benzene in a randomized trial of broccoli sprout beverage in Qidong, China
references.finding: Full-dose broccoli sprout beverage (~25 umol/d urinary sulforaphane metabolites) raised benzene detoxification by 63%; half and one-fifth doses had no significant effect.

references.authors: Kensler TW, Chen JG, Egner PA, et al.
references.title: Effects of glucosinolate-rich broccoli sprouts on urinary levels of aflatoxin-DNA adducts and phenanthrene tetraols in a randomized clinical trial in He Zuo township, Qidong, People's Republic of China
references.finding: Broccoli sprout infusion (400 umol glucoraphanin) for 2 weeks had no overall effect on aflatoxin-DNA adducts, but adducts were inversely related to individual sulforaphane metabolite excretion.

references.authors: Riedl MA, Saxon A, Diaz-Sanchez D
references.title: Oral sulforaphane increases Phase II antioxidant enzymes in the human upper airway
references.finding: Oral sulforaphane from broccoli sprout homogenate dose-dependently increased GSTM1, GSTP1, NQO1 and HO-1 expression in nasal cells, maximal at 200 g sprouts.

references.authors: Atwell LL, Hsu A, Wong CP, et al.
references.title: Absorption and chemopreventive targets of sulforaphane in humans following consumption of broccoli sprouts or a myrosinase-treated broccoli sprout extract
references.finding: Fresh sprouts gave ~3x higher sulforaphane exposure than a myrosinase-treated extract at 200 umol/d; no dose responses were seen for HO-1, HDAC activity or p21 in blood cells.

references.authors: Fahey JW, Wehage SL, Holtzclaw WD, et al.
references.title: Protection of humans by plant glucosinolates: efficiency of conversion of glucosinolates to isothiocyanates by the gastrointestinal microflora
references.finding: Gut microbial conversion of glucoraphanin to isothiocyanates varied from ~1% to >40% of dose between people but was consistent within individuals; sulforaphane itself was 70-90% recovered.

references.authors: Fahey JW, Holtzclaw WD, Wehage SL, et al.
references.title: Sulforaphane Bioavailability from Glucoraphanin-Rich Broccoli: Control by Active Endogenous Myrosinase
references.finding: Sprouts or seeds with active myrosinase gave 3-4 fold more sulforaphane bioavailability than glucoraphanin without active myrosinase.

references.authors: Cramer JM, Teran-Garcia M, Jeffery EH
references.title: Enhancing sulforaphane absorption and excretion in healthy men through the combined consumption of fresh broccoli sprouts and a glucoraphanin-rich powder
references.finding: Combining fresh broccoli sprouts with a glucoraphanin powder recovered 65% of the dose versus 60% (sprouts) and 24% (powder) and gave earlier sulforaphane appearance.

references.authors: Gasper AV, Al-Janobi A, Smith JA, et al.
references.title: Glutathione S-transferase M1 polymorphism and metabolism of sulforaphane from standard and high-glucosinolate broccoli
references.finding: GSTM1-null subjects had slightly higher plasma sulforaphane AUC and faster urinary excretion than GSTM1-positive subjects after eating broccoli.

references.authors: London SJ, Yuan JM, Chung FL, et al.
references.title: Isothiocyanates, glutathione S-transferase M1 and T1 polymorphisms, and lung-cancer risk: a prospective study of men in Shanghai, China
references.n: 232 lung cancer cases and 710 controls nested in 18,244 men
references.finding: Detectable urinary isothiocyanates were linked to lower lung cancer risk (RR 0.65), most strongly in GSTM1-null (0.36) and GSTM1/GSTT1 double-null men (0.28).

references.authors: Steck SE, Gammon MD, Hebert JR, et al.
references.title: GSTM1, GSTT1, GSTP1, and GSTA1 polymorphisms and urinary isothiocyanate metabolites following broccoli consumption in humans
references.finding: GST genotypes did not substantially change urinary isothiocyanate excretion after broccoli; GSTM1-null subjects were more often high excreters (62% vs 39%).

references.authors: Yagishita Y, Fahey JW, Dinkova-Kostova AT, et al.
references.title: Broccoli or Sulforaphane: Is It the Source or Dose That Matters?
references.finding: Reviews the relationships between broccoli/sprout/supplement formulation, sulforaphane bioavailability, dose and efficacy across >50 clinical trials.

references.authors: Gems D, Partridge L
references.title: Stress-response hormesis and aging: "that which does not kill us makes us stronger"
references.finding: Stress-response hormesis: sublethal stressors induce protective responses that can extend lifespan in animal models.

references.authors: Howitz KT, Sinclair DA
references.title: Xenohormesis: sensing the chemical cues of other species
references.finding: Proposes xenohormesis: animals sense plant stress molecules as cues to activate their own defences.

references.authors: Ristow M
references.title: Unraveling the truth about antioxidants: mitohormesis explains ROS-induced health benefits
references.finding: Argues that ROS-induced mitochondrial hormesis (mitohormesis) explains health benefits of exercise and caloric restriction and why antioxidants can block them.

references.authors: Ristow M, Zarse K, Oberbach A, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants prevent health-promoting effects of physical exercise in humans
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Vitamin C 1,000 mg/d plus vitamin E 400 IU/d during 4 weeks of exercise training abolished the training-induced gains in insulin sensitivity and endogenous antioxidant gene expression.

references.authors: Gomez-Cabrera MC, Domenech E, Romagnoli M, et al.
references.title: Oral administration of vitamin C decreases muscle mitochondrial biogenesis and hampers training-induced adaptations in endurance performance
references.finding: Vitamin C 1 g/d hampered training-induced endurance gains and blocked expression of mitochondrial biogenesis factors and antioxidant enzymes.

references.authors: Merry TL, Ristow M
references.title: Do antioxidant supplements interfere with skeletal muscle adaptation to exercise training?
references.finding: No convincing evidence that antioxidant supplements enhance training adaptations; they more consistently impair responses to resistance and high-intensity training.

references.authors: Michailidis Y, Karagounis LG, Terzis G, et al.
references.title: Thiol-based antioxidant supplementation alters human skeletal muscle signaling and attenuates its inflammatory response and recovery after intense eccentric exercise
references.finding: NAC raised muscle glutathione but blunted redox-sensitive signalling (Akt/mTOR/p70S6K), inflammation and recovery after eccentric exercise.

references.authors: Kadiiska MB, Gladen BC, Baird DD, et al.
references.title: Biomarkers of oxidative stress study II: are oxidation products of lipids, proteins, and DNA markers of CCl4 poisoning?
references.finding: BOSS study: in CCl4-poisoned rats, plasma/urinary F2-isoprostanes and MDA (GC-MS) and urinary 8-OHdG rose consistently; TBARS, protein carbonyls and others did not.

references.authors: Kadiiska MB, Peddada S, Herbert RA, et al.
references.title: Biomarkers of oxidative stress study VI. Endogenous plasma antioxidants fail as useful biomarkers of endotoxin-induced oxidative stress
references.finding: BOSS VI: plasma antioxidants (ascorbate, tocopherols, GSH/GSSG, total antioxidant capacity) failed as biomarkers of endotoxin-induced oxidative stress.

references.authors: Milne GL, Musiek ES, Morrow JD
references.title: F2-isoprostanes as markers of oxidative stress in vivo: an overview
references.finding: F2-isoprostanes, formed by free-radical peroxidation of arachidonic acid, are extremely accurate in vivo markers of lipid peroxidation when properly measured.

references.authors: Tsikas D
references.title: Assessment of lipid peroxidation by measuring malondialdehyde (MDA) and relatives in biological samples: Analytical and biological challenges
references.finding: Measuring MDA, HNE and 8-iso-PGF2a is analytically challenging; many methods, especially non-specific ones, are prone to artefacts.

references.authors: Dalle-Donne I, Rossi R, Giustarini D, et al.
references.title: Protein carbonyl groups as biomarkers of oxidative stress
references.finding: Protein carbonyls are relatively stable markers of protein oxidation, usually measured after DNPH derivatisation; their link to disease remains uncertain.

references.authors: Collins AR, Cadet J, Möller L, et al.
references.title: Are we sure we know how to measure 8-oxo-7,8-dihydroguanine in DNA from human cells?
references.finding: ESCODD found major inter-laboratory disagreement in DNA 8-oxoguanine due to artefactual oxidation; true background is ~0.3-4.2 per 10^6 guanines.

references.authors: Graille M, Wild P, Sauvain JJ, et al.
references.title: Urinary 8-OHdG as a Biomarker for Oxidative Stress: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
references.finding: Background urinary 8-OHdG in healthy adults (chemical methods) is ~3.9 ng/mg creatinine; smoking is associated with higher levels.

references.authors: Giustarini D, Dalle-Donne I, Milzani A, et al.
references.title: Analysis of GSH and GSSG after derivatization with N-ethylmaleimide
references.finding: Artefactual GSH oxidation during acid deproteinisation markedly overestimates GSSG unless GSH is first derivatised with N-ethylmaleimide.

references.authors: Tsimikas S, Brilakis ES, Miller ER, et al.
references.title: Oxidized phospholipids, Lp(a) lipoprotein, and coronary artery disease
references.finding: Oxidised phospholipids on apoB-100 (an oxidised LDL measure) were strongly associated with angiographic coronary artery disease, especially at age 60 or younger.

references.authors: Sies H
references.title: Total antioxidant capacity: appraisal of a concept
references.finding: Critique of 'total antioxidant capacity': summed assay values lack a coherent chemical or biological meaning.

references.authors: Lotito SB, Frei B
references.title: Consumption of flavonoid-rich foods and increased plasma antioxidant capacity in humans: cause, consequence, or epiphenomenon?
references.finding: The rise in plasma total antioxidant capacity after flavonoid-rich foods is not caused by flavonoids but likely by increased uric acid.

references.authors: Cunningham E
references.title: What has happened to the ORAC database?
references.finding: Explains USDA's 2012 withdrawal of its ORAC database: in-vitro antioxidant capacity has no demonstrated relevance to in-vivo effects and values were misused in marketing.

references.authors: Morrow JD, Frei B, Longmire AW, et al.
references.title: Increase in circulating products of lipid peroxidation (F2-isoprostanes) in smokers. Smoking as a cause of oxidative damage
references.finding: Plasma F2-isoprostanes were about twice as high in smokers and fell significantly after 2 weeks of smoking abstinence.

references.authors: Keaney JF Jr, Larson MG, Vasan RS, et al.
references.title: Obesity and systemic oxidative stress: clinical correlates of oxidative stress in the Framingham Study
references.finding: Urinary 8-epi-PGF2a was independently associated with smoking, BMI, blood glucose/diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

references.authors: Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta Carotene Cancer Prevention Study Group
references.title: The effect of vitamin E and beta carotene on the incidence of lung cancer and other cancers in male smokers
references.finding: Beta-carotene 20 mg/d increased lung cancer incidence by 18% and total mortality by 8%; alpha-tocopherol 50 mg/d did not reduce lung cancer and was linked to more hemorrhagic-stroke deaths.

references.authors: Omenn GS, Goodman GE, Thornquist MD, et al.
references.title: Effects of a combination of beta carotene and vitamin A on lung cancer and cardiovascular disease
references.finding: Beta-carotene 30 mg + retinol 25,000 IU increased lung cancer (RR 1.28) and all-cause mortality (RR 1.17); stopped early.

references.authors: Lippman SM, Klein EA, Goodman PJ, et al.
references.title: Effect of selenium and vitamin E on risk of prostate cancer and other cancers: the Selenium and Vitamin E Cancer Prevention Trial (SELECT)
references.finding: Selenium 200 ug/d and/or vitamin E 400 IU/d did not prevent prostate or other cancers; non-significant increases in prostate cancer (vitamin E) and diabetes (selenium).

references.authors: Klein EA, Thompson IM Jr, Tangen CM, et al.
references.title: Vitamin E and the risk of prostate cancer: the Selenium and Vitamin E Cancer Prevention Trial (SELECT)
references.finding: With extended follow-up, vitamin E 400 IU/d significantly increased prostate cancer risk (HR 1.17).

references.authors: Kristal AR, Darke AK, Morris JS, et al.
references.title: Baseline selenium status and effects of selenium and vitamin e supplementation on prostate cancer risk
references.finding: Selenium raised high-grade prostate cancer by 91% in men with high baseline selenium; vitamin E raised prostate cancer risk in men with low selenium.

references.authors: HOPE Study Investigators (Yusuf S, et al.)
references.title: Vitamin E supplementation and cardiovascular events in high-risk patients
references.finding: Vitamin E 400 IU/d for 4.5 years had no effect on cardiovascular events (RR 1.05).

references.authors: Lonn E, Bosch J, Yusuf S, et al.
references.title: Effects of long-term vitamin E supplementation on cardiovascular events and cancer: a randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Long-term vitamin E 400 IU/d did not prevent cancer or major CV events and increased heart failure (RR 1.13).

references.authors: Sesso HD, Buring JE, Christen WG, et al.
references.title: Vitamins E and C in the prevention of cardiovascular disease in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Vitamin E 400 IU every other day and vitamin C 500 mg/d for 8 years had no effect on major CV events; vitamin E increased hemorrhagic stroke (HR 1.74).

references.authors: Gaziano JM, Glynn RJ, Christen WG, et al.
references.title: Vitamins E and C in the prevention of prostate and total cancer in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Neither vitamin E nor vitamin C reduced prostate or total cancer over 8 years.

references.authors: Heart Protection Study Collaborative Group
references.title: MRC/BHF Heart Protection Study of antioxidant vitamin supplementation in 20,536 high-risk individuals: a randomised placebo-controlled trial
references.finding: Vitamin E 600 mg + vitamin C 250 mg + beta-carotene 20 mg daily raised blood levels but had no effect on vascular events, cancer or mortality over 5 years.

references.authors: Lee IM, Cook NR, Gaziano JM, et al.
references.title: Vitamin E in the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease and cancer: the Women's Health Study: a randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Vitamin E 600 IU every other day gave no overall benefit for CV events, cancer or total mortality; CV death was 24% lower (secondary outcome).

references.authors: Bjelakovic G, Nikolova D, Gluud LL, et al.
references.title: Antioxidant supplements for prevention of mortality in healthy participants and patients with various diseases
references.finding: Antioxidant supplements increased mortality in low-bias trials (RR 1.04); beta-carotene (RR 1.05) and vitamin E (RR 1.03) significantly, vitamin C and selenium not.

references.authors: Miller ER 3rd, Pastor-Barriuso R, Dalal D, et al.
references.title: Meta-analysis: high-dosage vitamin E supplementation may increase all-cause mortality
references.finding: High-dose vitamin E (>=400 IU/d) increased all-cause mortality by 39 per 10,000; risk rose above ~150 IU/d.

references.authors: Schürks M, Glynn RJ, Rist PM, et al.
references.title: Effects of vitamin E on stroke subtypes: meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
references.finding: Vitamin E increased hemorrhagic stroke by 22% and reduced ischemic stroke by 10%, with no effect on total stroke.

references.authors: Druesne-Pecollo N, Latino-Martel P, Norat T, et al.
references.title: Beta-carotene supplementation and cancer risk: a systematic review and metaanalysis of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: Beta-carotene had no effect on overall cancer but at 20-30 mg/d increased lung (RR 1.16) and stomach cancer, especially in smokers and asbestos workers.

references.authors: Liu C, Wang XD, Bronson RT, et al.
references.title: Effects of physiological versus pharmacological beta-carotene supplementation on cell proliferation and histopathological changes in the lungs of cigarette smoke-exposed ferrets
references.finding: In smoke-exposed ferrets, pharmacological beta-carotene (~30 mg/d human equivalent) lowered lung retinoic acid and caused squamous metaplasia; a physiological dose (~6 mg/d) did not.

references.authors: Sayin VI, Ibrahim MX, Larsson E, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants accelerate lung cancer progression in mice
references.finding: NAC and vitamin E accelerated lung tumour progression and shortened survival in mice by reducing ROS, DNA damage and p53 expression.

references.authors: Le Gal K, Ibrahim MX, Wiel C, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants can increase melanoma metastasis in mice
references.finding: NAC and Trolox increased lymph node metastasis of melanoma in mice by raising tumour-cell glutathione and RHOA activation.

references.authors: Roberts LJ 2nd, Oates JA, Linton MF, et al.
references.title: The relationship between dose of vitamin E and suppression of oxidative stress in humans
references.finding: Vitamin E lowered plasma F2-isoprostanes significantly only at 1,600 IU/d (-35%) and 3,200 IU/d (-49%), with maximum effect after 16 weeks.

references.authors: Meagher EA, Barry OP, Lawson JA, et al.
references.title: Effects of vitamin E on lipid peroxidation in healthy persons
references.finding: Vitamin E 200-2,000 IU/d for 8 weeks raised vitamin E levels but did not change urinary isoprostanes or 4-HNE.

references.authors: US Preventive Services Task Force, Mangione CM, Barry MJ, et al.

references.title: Multivitamins in the prevention of cancer in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
references.finding: A daily multivitamin for 11 years modestly reduced total cancer (HR 0.92).

references.title: Vitamin C pharmacokinetics in healthy volunteers: evidence for a recommended dietary allowance

references.authors: Thomas LD, Elinder CG, Tiselius HG, et al.

references.title: Dietary (poly)phenolics in human health: structures, bioavailability, and evidence of protective effects against chronic diseases

references.authors: Halliwell B
references.title: The antioxidant paradox: less paradoxical now?

references.finding: Plasma and cells saturated at 400 mg/day; F2-isoprostanes did not change at any vitamin C dose in these replete women.

references.authors: Loftfield E, O'Connell CP, Abnet CC, et al.
references.title: Multivitamin Use and Mortality Risk in 3 Prospective US Cohorts
references.finding: Daily multivitamin use was not associated with lower mortality (HR 1.04 in the first half of follow-up).

references.authors: Martí-Carvajal AJ, Solà I, Lathyris D, et al.
references.title: Homocysteine-lowering interventions for preventing cardiovascular events
references.finding: Cochrane: B-vitamin homocysteine lowering did not reduce MI or death but modestly reduced stroke (RR 0.90).

references.authors: McNulty H, Pentieva K, Ward M
references.title: Causes and Clinical Sequelae of Riboflavin Deficiency
references.finding: Subclinical riboflavin deficiency may be widespread even in high-income countries but goes undetected; linked to anaemia and hypertension.

references.authors: Mills JL, Buck Louis GM, Kannan K, et al.
references.title: Delayed conception in women with low-urinary iodine concentrations: a population-based prospective cohort study
references.finding: Women with iodine:creatinine <50 ug/g had 46% lower fecundability per cycle (OR 0.54).

references.authors: Ni Z, Li Y, Song D, et al.
references.title: Iron-overloaded follicular fluid increases the risk of endometriosis-related infertility by triggering granulosa cell ferroptosis and oocyte dysmaturity
references.finding: Iron-overloaded follicular fluid from women with endometriosis triggered granulosa-cell ferroptosis and impaired oocyte maturation in mouse models; vitamin E and deferoxamine helped.

references.authors: Nielsen FH, Johnson LK, Zeng H
references.title: Magnesium supplementation improves indicators of low magnesium status and inflammatory stress in adults older than 51 years with poor quality sleep
references.finding: 320 mg/day magnesium lowered CRP only in those with baseline CRP >3 mg/L; 58% ate below the magnesium EAR.

references.authors: Niklewicz A, Hannibal L, Warren M, et al.
references.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of functional vitamin B12 status among adult vegans
references.finding: Vegans had lower serum B12 and higher homocysteine and methylmalonic acid than omnivores, indicating functional B12 deficiency.

references.authors: O'Connor EA, Evans CV, Ivlev I, et al.
references.title: Vitamin and Mineral Supplements for the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force
references.finding: Multivitamins were associated with slightly lower cancer incidence (OR 0.93, 4 RCTs) with important limitations; beta-carotene raised lung cancer; limited evidence linked vitamin A to hip fracture, vitamin E to hemorrhagic stroke and vitamin C to kidney stones.

references.authors: Passarelli S, Free CM, Shepon A, et al.
references.title: Global estimation of dietary micronutrient inadequacies: a modelling analysis
references.finding: From food alone, >5 billion people under-consume iodine, vitamin E and calcium and >4 billion under-consume iron, riboflavin, folate and vitamin C.

references.authors: Rayman MP
references.title: Selenium and human health
references.finding: Selenium's health effects follow a U-shaped curve: extra intake may help people with low status but those with adequate-to-high status may be harmed.

references.authors: Rayman MP, Winther KH, Pastor-Barriuso R, et al.
references.title: Effect of long-term selenium supplementation on mortality: Results from a multiple-dose, randomised controlled trial
references.finding: 300 ug/day selenium for 5 years raised all-cause mortality over 10 years (HR 1.59, 1.02-2.46); 100 and 200 ug showed no harm.

references.authors: Safarinejad MR, Safarinejad S
references.title: Efficacy of selenium and/or N-acetyl-cysteine for improving semen parameters in infertile men: a double-blind, placebo controlled, randomized study
references.finding: Reported that 200 ug selenium and/or 600 mg NAC improved all semen parameters; the journal issued an Expression of Concern in 2023.

references.authors: Schisterman EF, Sjaarda LA, Clemons T, et al.
references.title: Effect of Folic Acid and Zinc Supplementation in Men on Semen Quality and Live Birth Among Couples Undergoing Infertility Treatment: A Randomized Clinical Trial
references.n: 2370 men in couples seeking infertility care (FAZST)
references.finding: 5 mg folic acid plus 30 mg zinc for 6 months did not improve semen quality or live birth (34% vs 35%) and slightly raised sperm DNA fragmentation (+2.4 points).

references.authors: Schleicher RL, Carroll MD, Ford ES, et al.
references.title: Serum vitamin C and the prevalence of vitamin C deficiency in the United States: 2003-2004 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES)
references.finding: 7.1% of the US population was vitamin C deficient; smokers had about one-third lower concentrations.

references.authors: Scott R, MacPherson A, Yates RW, et al.
references.title: The effect of oral selenium supplementation on human sperm motility
references.n: 69 subfertile Scottish men with low selenium status
references.finding: Selenium (100 ug/day) for 3 months raised sperm motility vs placebo; 11% achieved paternity vs none on placebo.

references.authors: Sesso HD, Christen WG, Bubes V, et al.
references.title: Multivitamins in the prevention of cardiovascular disease in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
references.finding: A daily multivitamin did not reduce major cardiovascular events (HR 1.01) or total mortality (HR 0.94).

references.authors: Sesso HD, Rist PM, Aragaki AK, et al.
references.title: Multivitamins in the prevention of cancer and cardiovascular disease: the COcoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study (COSMOS) randomized clinical trial
references.finding: A daily multivitamin for a median 3.6 years did not reduce total cancer (HR 0.97) or CVD (HR 0.98); lung cancer was lower (HR 0.62).

references.authors: Sohn SY, Inoue K, Rhee CM, et al.
references.title: Risks of Iodine Excess
references.finding: Excess iodine (supplements, contrast media, amiodarone) can trigger hypo- or hyperthyroidism in susceptible people.

references.authors: Srinutta T, Chewcharat A, Takkavatakarn K, et al.
references.title: Proton pump inhibitors and hypomagnesemia: A meta-analysis of observational studies
references.finding: PPI use was associated with hypomagnesaemia (adjusted OR 1.71), more with high doses (OR 2.13).

references.authors: Stagnaro-Green A, Pearce EN
references.title: Iodine and pregnancy: a call to action
references.finding: Lancet comment calling for action on iodine nutrition in pregnancy.

references.authors: Stampfer M, Willett W
references.title: Folate supplements for stroke prevention: targeted trial trumps the rest
references.finding: JAMA editorial arguing that the CSPPT targeted trial in a low-folate population outweighs earlier null trials in fortified populations.

references.authors: Stockwell BR, Friedmann Angeli JP, Bayir H, et al.
references.title: Ferroptosis: A Regulated Cell Death Nexus Linking Metabolism, Redox Biology, and Disease
references.finding: Ferroptosis review: iron, polyunsaturated lipid peroxidation and loss of GPX4/glutathione defences link metabolism, redox biology and disease.

references.authors: Stranges S, Marshall JR, Natarajan R, et al.
references.title: Effects of long-term selenium supplementation on the incidence of type 2 diabetes: a randomized trial
references.finding: 200 ug/day selenium raised type 2 diabetes (HR 1.55), highest in the top baseline selenium tertile (HR 2.70).

references.authors: Ursini F, Heim S, Kiess M, et al.
references.title: Dual function of the selenoprotein PHGPx during sperm maturation
references.finding: The selenoprotein PHGPx (GPX4) becomes a structural protein making up >=50% of the sperm midpiece mitochondrial capsule, explaining midpiece fragility in selenium deficiency.

references.authors: Mangione CM, Barry MJ, Nicholson WK, et al.
references.title: Vitamin, Mineral, and Multivitamin Supplementation to Prevent Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
references.finding: USPSTF: insufficient evidence for multivitamins to prevent CVD or cancer; recommends against beta-carotene and vitamin E.

references.authors: Barry MJ, Nicholson WK, Silverstein M, et al.
references.title: Folic Acid Supplementation to Prevent Neural Tube Defects: US Preventive Services Task Force Reaffirmation Recommendation Statement
references.finding: USPSTF (A recommendation): everyone who could become pregnant should take 400-800 ug folic acid daily.

references.authors: Veronese N, Pizzol D, Smith L, et al.
references.title: Effect of Magnesium Supplementation on Inflammatory Parameters: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
references.finding: Magnesium supplements lowered serum CRP and raised nitric oxide.

references.authors: Vinceti M, Filippini T, Del Giovane C, et al.
references.title: Selenium for preventing cancer
references.finding: Cochrane: selenium supplements did not prevent cancer (RR 1.01, high certainty).

references.authors: Vyas CM, Manson JE, Sesso HD, et al.
references.title: Effect of multivitamin-mineral supplementation versus placebo on cognitive function: results from the clinic subcohort of the COcoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study (COSMOS) randomized clinical trial and meta-analysis of 3 cognitive studies within COSMOS
references.n: 573 COSMOS-Clinic participants plus meta-analysis of 3 COSMOS cohorts
references.finding: A multivitamin improved episodic memory over 2 years; pooled COSMOS data showed small benefits on global cognition (0.07 SD).

references.authors: Wessells KR, Brown KH
references.title: Estimating the global prevalence of zinc deficiency: results based on zinc availability in national food supplies and the prevalence of stunting
references.finding: An estimated 17.3% of the world's population is at risk of inadequate zinc intake, highest in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.

references.authors: Wilson CP, McNulty H, Ward M, et al.
references.title: Blood pressure in treated hypertensive individuals with the MTHFR 677TT genotype is responsive to intervention with riboflavin: findings of a targeted randomized trial
references.finding: 1.6 mg/day riboflavin for 16 weeks lowered systolic BP by 5.6 mmHg vs placebo in this genotype.

references.authors: Zhao J, Dong X, Hu X, et al.
references.title: Zinc levels in seminal plasma and their correlation with male infertility: A systematic review and meta-analysis
references.finding: Infertile men had lower seminal zinc; pooled small trials suggested zinc improved volume, motility and morphology.

references.authors: Zhou H, Wang T, Li Q, et al.
references.title: Prevention of Keshan Disease by Selenium Supplementation: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
references.finding: Selenium supplementation in endemic areas cut Keshan disease (selenium-deficiency cardiomyopathy) incidence by 86% (RR 0.14).
